headline: Iran’s supreme leader orders maximum response to any US attack
description: TEHRAN/WASHINGTON - Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday reportedly warned the United States and Israel against returning to war,
author: Monitoring Desk
article_text:
TEHRAN/WASHINGTON - Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday reportedly warned the United States and Israel against returning to war, according to a written statement, following threats from Tehran’s foes of a possible resumption of strikes, which a report said could come as early as November 4, the day after the US midterms. “If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them,” according to a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his website. The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them. Khamenei has not been publicly seen since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s killing in the opening strikes of the war on February 28. The younger Khamenei is believed to have been injured in a US-Israeli strike the same day his father was killed. According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response.” It also said that Khamenei ordered the commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy.” Iran launched thousands of drones and missiles during this year’s war, targeting Israel, US bases in the region, as well as energy sites throughout the Middle East. It also managed to shoot a missile at the Diego Garcia air base some 4,000 kilometers (2,500 miles) away in the southern Indian Ocean, signaling its ability to fire at nearly anywhere in Europe. Israeli officials have repeatedly warned of the Iranian threat to Europe, and several European countries have said that they believe Iran is behind a series of attacks and plots against Jewish targets throughout the continent. Joining in on the threats was the Iranian Armed Forces, which warned Saturday that any new US attack would only spread their war wider. “If the US president once again embarks on more regional adventurism under pressure from, and in an attempt to appease, the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said in a post on X, without elaborating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also warned on Saturday that “Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people.”

Also, Iran’s top diplomat says there are no plans to hold talks with the United States despite growing concerns over a return to war. “Currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials, and any speculation to the contrary is merely media assumption,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA. The statements came as fresh diplomatic efforts were underway to avert a resumption of fighting. A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials, after Iran reportedly received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance. According to Iranian media, Tehran had yet to respond to the letter. Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said he’s “extremely worried” that a new round of escalation in the war between the United States and Iran would be more destructive and have a major impact, speaking at the IISS Manama Dialogue security summit in Bahrain. Parallel to the talks, Washington warned Gulf allies to prepare for a possible new round of strikes on Iran as early as November 4, a day after the US midterm elections, MSNOW reported Saturday, citing three senior Gulf Arab officials familiar with the discussions. The strikes are expected to be brief but intense, according to the officials, who said the Gulf states are pressing Washington to de-escalate amid fears of Iranian retaliation. One official said they “would not be surprised” if some Gulf countries opposed the use of American military bases on their territory to launch the attacks. The US has not struck Iran since September 1, while US President Donald Trump has pledged to refrain from further attacks until after the midterms. Asked about the reported plans, a White House official told MSNOW that “we do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist,” adding that Trump “keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.” “He’s obsessed with Iran not getting a nuclear weapon,” a former Trump administration official familiar with White House foreign policy deliberations told the outlet. “He’s been convinced that with this final attack we can get a deal with the Iranians, or we can finally destroy their nuclear program.” Meanwhile, Iran said two fishermen it had reported missing on Saturday have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. “Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found,” state television said. Earlier, state TV had cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway. US Central Command (CENTCOM) did not immediately comment on the reported strike. The White House and the Pentagon also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said he’s “extremely worried” that a new round of escalation in the war between the United States and Iran would be more destructive and have a major impact, speaking at the IISS Manama Dialogue security summit in Bahrain.

Parallel to the talks, Washington warned Gulf allies to prepare for a possible new round of strikes on Iran as early as November 4, a day after the US midterm elections, MSNOW reported Saturday, citing three senior Gulf Arab officials familiar with the discussions.

The strikes are expected to be brief but intense, according to the officials, who said the Gulf states are pressing Washington to de-escalate amid fears of Iranian retaliation.

One official said they “would not be surprised” if some Gulf countries opposed the use of American military bases on their territory to launch the attacks.

The US has not struck Iran since September 1, while US President Donald Trump has pledged to refrain from further attacks until after the midterms.

Asked about the reported plans, a White House official told MSNOW that “we do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist,” adding that Trump “keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.”

“He’s obsessed with Iran not getting a nuclear weapon,” a former Trump administration official familiar with White House foreign policy deliberations told the outlet. “He’s been convinced that with this final attack we can get a deal with the Iranians, or we can finally destroy their nuclear program.”

Meanwhile, Iran said two fishermen it had reported missing on Saturday have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found,” state television said.

Earlier, state TV had cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) did not immediately comment on the reported strike. The White House and the Pentagon also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

headline: Centre saved KP from PTI’s poor governance: PM
description: ISLAMABAD - Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday called upon the provincial leadership of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text: ISLAMABAD - Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday called upon the provincial leadership of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to urgently prioritise short-term, public welfare-oriented initiatives, asserting that local residents have suffered years of developmental neglect. Addressing a gathering of the PML-N KP chapter, the prime minister criticised the past PTI-led administration’s governance record, saying that despite tall claims of revolutionary reforms in the education and health sectors, citizens continued to yearn for basic facilities. He regretted that PTI’s political focus was diverted toward protests and sit-ins rather than addressing the socio-economic needs of the province. “How many development projects were completed? Were public funds spent judiciously, and what steps were taken against corruption?” the prime minister questioned, raising concerns over transparency and the execution of past provincial policies. Turning to national security, the prime minister paid rich tribute to the immense sacrifices rendered by the residents of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, law enforcement agencies, and the armed forces in eradicating terrorism during the period of 2017–2018. He noted that the country lost approximately 80,000 precious lives, with economic losses mounting between $150 billion and $200 billion in the long fight against terrorism. He specifically recalled the tragic attack on the Army Public School (APS) in Peshawar as an unforgettable manifestation of barbarism, while also acknowledging the sacrifices borne by political figures and security personnel. Reflecting on past political and economic milestones, the prime minister criticised the 2014 PTI’s sit-ins, noting that they coincided with and delayed the historic visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. He contrasted this with the subsequent signing of major bilateral agreements in 2015 and the eventual elimination of crippling, hours-long load-shedding under the leadership of Nawaz Sharif. Furthermore, the prime minister expressed deep concern over security challenges witnessed in subsequent years, emphasizing the need for sustained vigilance, economic uplift, and grassroots development to deliver tangible relief to the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. About Governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), he described the measure as an unavoidable step to protect the state, economy, and the welfare of the provincial populace. Addressing party leaders, the prime minister pointed back to the 2010 National Finance Commission (NFC) Award—concluded under then-Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani with unanimous consensus from all chief ministers—which allocated a 1 percent financial share directly to KP. He noted that the province has accrued approximately Rs 800 billion from this arrangement over the years. Questioning the transparency of fund utilisation, the prime minister asked how much of that allocation was genuinely invested into reinforcing the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and local law enforcement. Had those resources been properly managed, he argued, the provincial police force would have been significantly better equipped to tackle security challenges. About 8,000 police vacancies were lying in the province. Addressing the broader macroeconomic environment, the prime minister acknowledged that ongoing crises in the Gulf region have driven global energy costs upward. However, he emphasised that the federal government has ensured uninterrupted supplies of petrol and diesel across the country. He highlighted the launch of a targeted fuel subsidy program in February, backed by Rs 75 billion allocation, which has successfully delivered relief vouchers to approximately 130 million citizens. Detailing the breakdown in political negotiations he said, the federal government made concerted efforts to engage the PTI leadership in KP to address pressing national challenges cooperatively. According to the premier, after negotiations led by a joint PML-N and PPP delegation, the finalised draft proposals faced outright delay from Sohail Afridi, leaving them with no alternative course of action. “We had no other option but to save the country, the economy, the society, and KP,” he warned, stressing that further hesitation would have led to catastrophic outcomes. The prime minister also outlined ongoing projects to build Daanish Schools across remote districts—including Chitral, Haripur, Mansehra, Bajaur, and Shangla—with plans to announce several additional campuses later in the year. Earlier, Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan, Engineer Amir Muqam, in his remarks, said the PML-N enjoyed a massive public support in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as it always overcame challenges. Meanwhile, PM Shehbaz Sharif has directed the authorities to accelerate construction of Daanish Schools across the country, ensuring round-the-clock work for their timely completion, while stressing that no compromise on their quality standards would be acceptable. He was chairing a review meeting on Saturday to assess progress on the construction of Daanish Schools nationwide. “Our children are the future of the country, and Daanish Schools represent an investment in a bright future,” the prime minister said, adding that admission to these institutions would be granted strictly on merit to children belonging to the poorest and most deserving families. He directed the relevant authorities to adopt modern artificial intelligence (AI) and information technology (IT)-based methods for the education and training of students to equip them with contemporary knowledge and skills. The prime minister also ordered third-party validation to assess the quality of infrastructure, facilities and services being provided at Daanish Schools. Directing the Ministry of Communications, he called for establishing an efficient road network to ensure easy access to Daanish Schools in Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). He further directed the authorities to present a strategy for establishing Daanish Schools in the merged districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (formerly FATA) at the earliest. During the meeting, the prime minister was briefed on the progress of construction of Daanish Schools in Gilgit-Baltistan, AJK, Sindh and Balochistan. Federal Ministers Ahsan Iqbal, Ahad Khan Cheema, Attaullah Tarar, Shaza Fatima Khawaja and Dr Musadik Masood Malik, along with senior officials of the relevant departments and institutions, attended the meeting, which was held online through Zoom.

headline: 14-year-old boy killed in shell explosion in Lakki Marwat
description: PESHAWAR - A 14-year-old boy was killed when a shell exploded near his house in Sarband Wanda Mir Wali area of Lakki Marwat early Saturday morning. Police said
author: NEWS WIRE
article_text: PESHAWAR - A 14-year-old boy was killed when a shell exploded near his house in Sarband Wanda Mir Wali area of Lakki Marwat early Saturday morning. Police said the victim, identified as Yaseen, had left his house to take livestock out for grazing when the shell landed nearby and killed him on the spot. The police shifted the body to City Hospital Lakki Marwat for medico-legal formalities. They have launched an investigation to determine the origin of the shell and establish where it was fired from. The incident has spread concern among local residents.

headline: Info minister proposes national council to counter digital threats
description: Islamabad - Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar has proposed the establishment of a National Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text: Islamabad - Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar has proposed the establishment of a National Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness Council to protect people from digital threats. He was addressing the inaugural ceremony of Cyber Security Awareness Week 2026, organised by Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) in Islamabad on Sturday. The Information Minister said provincial governments, federal ministries and divisions, as well as other organizations, could be members of the proposed council. He assured his full support for its establishment to ensure awareness initiatives are carried out at every level throughout the year. Attaullah Tarar said that, given the diverse aspects of cybersecurity, a more integrated and cohesive whole-of-government approach is needed to reach every citizen effectively. He emphasized the need to include digital literacy in the curricula at school, college and university levels to educate children about emerging technological threats and ways to address them. The Minister called for a research-based system in which the curriculum is regularly updated in line with rapidly evolving technology. He said digital literacy should be made compulsory for every citizen.

headline: 28th Constitutional Amendment: Talk the talk, but not walk the walk
description: ISLAMABAD - As the weather turns colder next month, the political temperature is likely to witness a heated political atmosphere with the possibility of
author: JAVAID UR RAHMAN
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - As the weather turns colder next month, the political temperature is likely to witness a heated political atmosphere with the possibility of legislation on 28th constitutional package opening doors to the creation of new provinces and administrative units. Though the political gossip on new administrative units remained on its peak in media platforms, it could not formally land in the parliament for formal legislation due to a plethora of reasons. This constitutional package is not only accepted by the opposition factions but also the main coalition partners are not on the same page with the ruling party [PML-N].

Since the numerical strength is necessary for passing the legislative peace with 2/3 majority the main ruling cliques have not given a nod for redrawing geographical boundaries in the country. The ruling party had yet to initiate legislation for this new adventure mainly because of PPP’s cold shoulder on it. Whereas, the second main coalition partner [MQM-P] has assured its full support in and outside the parliament.

While talking to The Nation, Minister for parliamentary affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhary said the government has not finalised tabling the constitutional package in the parliament for legislation. “Obviously, the constitutional package will be approved with the consent of all partners. We [PML-N] will discuss all the coalition partners before properly launching it in the parliament,” he commented.

To a question about approving the 28th constitutional package in the month of December, the Minister said all the coalition partners will be taken into confidence. When contacted, PPP’s senior MNA Shazia Marri said Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) has not been taken into confidence over 28th constitutional amendment. “We don’t have any information on a new constitutional package,” she said, mentioning that the plan to bring amendments regarding new administrative units/provinces was not shared with them.

To a question regarding numerical strength to pass the constitutional amendment, Marri said, “There is importance of every single vote in the parliament for legislation,” she said, mentioning that the votes of PPP MNAs would be important for any legislative business.

Talking to this scribe, MQM-P’s MNA Dr Farooq Sattar said though the constitutional amendment passed with 2/3 majority yet this legislative piece might be approved with simple majority by passing a resolution moved by the Prime Minister.

“As do I suppose, a resolution will be moved through the Prime Minister to carry out a referendum under 48(6),” he said, mentioning that the Prime Minister can refer the matter to a joint sitting of Parliament (National Assembly and Senate). “Following approval, the Prime Minister may cause the matter to be referred to a public referendum,” he said, sharing a possible roadmap for the constitutional package.

The prospect of seeking opinion on the creation of new provinces was mainly started a couple of months ago.As, interior minister Mohsin Naqvi viewed that any new administrative units in the country would only be formed if the people voiced their support for such a move.

This political move is considered to be possible with the 2/3 majority in the parliament but a major political force (PPP) has strongly opposed the idea. A senior parliamentarian, desiring not to be named, said that there are slim chances to build consensus on this important issue.

Political pundits viewed that the PML-N would start proper work to convince coalition partners and the opposition factions in coming weeks. The ruling party would try to pass the amendment without adopting a referendum choice for the new administrative units.

headline: FESCO, GEPCO, IESCO privatisation most likely in first quarter of 2027: PM’s aide
description: ISLAMABAD - Prime Minister’s Adviser on Privatisation and Chairman of the Privatisation Commission Muhammad Ali has said that he government is planning
author: NEWS WIRE
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Prime Minister’s Adviser on Privatisation and Chairman of the Privatisation Commission Muhammad Ali has said that he government is planning to privatise three power distribution companies (DISCOs) during the first quarter of 2027. The Companies included Faisalabad Electric Supply Company (FESCO), Gujranwala Electric Power Company (GEPCO) and Islamabad Electric Supply Company (IESCO), he said in an interview, on Saturday. Muhammad Ali said that due diligence for the three companies was already underway, while potential investors had requested additional time to assess the complex transactions.

He said the government had initially planned to hold bidding in December, but the process might be delayed slightly, with the target now set for the first quarter of next year. The government has also started work on the privatisation of Hyderabad and Sukkur power distribution companies, with their transactions expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2027.

Lahore, Multan, Peshawar and Hazara distribution companies are also part of the government’s privatisation programme, with a target to complete their process in the second half of 2027.

Muhammad Ali described power sector reform as a national security issue, saying high energy costs were undermining industrial competitiveness, exports and economic growth.

He said Pakistan needed to reduce electricity tariffs and introduce competition in the power supply market to prevent consumers and industries from shifting away from the national grid.

Referring to the experience of K-Electric, he acknowledged that investors had raised concerns about regulatory uncertainty, tariff revisions and the protection of long-term investments.

He said the government was working on safeguards to address these concerns, including finalising investment plans and multi-year tariffs before bidding.

According to Muhammad Ali, DISCOs would be required to improve their performance through smart metering, technology adoption, reduction in electricity losses, better recovery, uninterrupted power supply and improved load management.

He said investors would face penalties for failing to meet performance benchmarks, while improved efficiency and reduced losses would be rewarded. The benefits of improved performance would also be shared with consumers.

The Privatisation Commission has prepared a comprehensive reform paper covering tariff structures, investment plans, business activities and the introduction of a competitive electricity market.

He said the government intended to share the reform proposals with the public by mid-November after consultations with relevant institutions, the Prime Minister and the Steering Committee.

The proposed reforms also aim to gradually move away from the uniform electricity tariff by introducing a competitive supplier system, while retaining a supplier of last resort for consumers unable to access competitive suppliers.

Muhammad Ali said investors would receive returns in Pakistani rupees rather than dollars, with returns linked to inflation and calculated under the capital asset pricing model.

He stressed that investors must receive a fair return on their investments, but the government would also ensure that consumers benefited from improvements in efficiency.

On employees’ concerns, he said the government would protect DISCO workers and provide a specific period during which investors would not be allowed to take adverse action against employees or change their employment terms.

He added that employees would remain essential to operating the electricity distribution system even after privatisation.

The adviser said the government was also examining the privatisation of Pakistan State Oil (PSO), Sui Southern Gas Company and Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited, while strategic activities of PSO could remain under government control.

He said the government was pursuing a broader privatisation programme aimed at improving efficiency, attracting investment and addressing structural challenges in key sectors of the economy.

headline: CM Maryam invites French investors to explore opportunities in Punjab’s agri, industrial sectors
description: LAHORE - Punjab Chief Minister Punjab Maryam Nawaz Sharif held a meeting with the new French Ambassador to Pakistan Jean-Noël Poirier to explore avenues
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
LAHORE - Punjab Chief Minister Punjab Maryam Nawaz Sharif held a meeting with the new French Ambassador to Pakistan Jean-Noël Poirier to explore avenues for strengthening bilateral relations, enhancing trade and investment and expanding industrial cooperation between Punjab and France.

The chief minister warmly welcomed the French ambassador on his arrival in Lahore, congratulated him on assuming his new diplomatic responsibilities and appreciated his diplomatic services.

During the meeting, both sides discussed opportunities to enhance economic, commercial and investment cooperation between Pakistan and France, with particular focus on developing stronger provincial-level partnerships between Punjab and French institutions.

The CM invited French investors to explore investment opportunities in Punjab’s agriculture, industrial and livestock sectors through the PIVOT initiative. She emphasised that greater engagement with French companies could open new avenues for industrial development, technology transfer and economic growth. The French ambassador invited the chief minister to visit France to explore opportunities for expanding bilateral trade and economic relations.

CM Maryam Nawaz thanked him for the invitation and expressed her interest in strengthening commercial and industrial ties between the two sides.

The meeting also focused on Pakistan’s GSP+ status and its significance for the country’s exports and industrial economy. The chief minister described the preferential trade arrangement as a lifeline for Pakistan’s exports, particularly for Punjab’s textile, garments, sports goods and leather industries, which depend heavily on access to European markets.

She stressed that France’s support was important for safeguarding Pakistan’s trade interests within the European Union and maintaining preferential access for Pakistani products. She said alignment with the requirements of the new GSP+ framework was essential for securing the country’s export prospects.

Maryam Nawaz noted that the European Union was Pakistan’s largest trading partner, with Pakistan’s exports to the bloc reaching approximately $8.96 billion in 2025-26. She underscored the importance of continued diplomatic engagement with France to strengthen Pakistan’s position on GSP+ and further consolidate trade relations with the EU.

Recalling France’s previous support for Pakistan’s GSP+ status at the ministerial level, CM Punjab expressed confidence that continued French cooperation would help protect Pakistan’s commercial interests in European markets.

The chief minister also thanked France for providing a €180 million loan for National Transmission and Despatch Company (NTDC) transmission lines and grid stations in Punjab, acknowledging the contribution towards strengthening the province’s energy infrastructure.

She invited French investors to benefit from investment opportunities in the Urban wastewater governance project planned for major cities of Punjab, highlighting the potential for international partnerships in urban infrastructure and environmental management.

Identifying specific areas of cooperation, Maryam Nawaz said French dairy, food-processing and cold-chain companies could help modernize agriculture and add value in Punjab. French utility companies could participate in water supply, wastewater management, sewerage and solid waste services under the public-private partnership model.

She further said French energy companies could explore opportunities in solar energy, grid infrastructure and energy-efficiency projects in industrial estates, while French institutions could assist in technical training and skills development for Punjab’s workforce through industrial clusters under PIVOT.

The CM observed that PIVOT could provide an effective platform for establishing direct institutional links between Punjab and France, creating new opportunities for industrial collaboration, investment and development partnerships.

Emphasising the longstanding friendship between Pakistan and France, Maryam Nawaz said the two countries shared decades of diplomatic relations and common aspirations for cooperation. Referring to the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, she appreciated France’s historic contribution to the principles of liberty, equality and human dignity.

She also commended France’s recognition of Palestine and its principled position on justice and equal rights.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations through sustained diplomatic engagement, increased trade, investment and industrial partnerships and cooperation in mutually beneficial areas of economic development.

The chief minister warmly welcomed the French ambassador on his arrival in Lahore, congratulated him on assuming his new diplomatic responsibilities and appreciated his diplomatic services.

During the meeting, both sides discussed opportunities to enhance economic, commercial and investment cooperation between Pakistan and France, with particular focus on developing stronger provincial-level partnerships between Punjab and French institutions.

The CM invited French investors to explore investment opportunities in Punjab’s agriculture, industrial and livestock sectors through the PIVOT initiative. She emphasised that greater engagement with French companies could open new avenues for industrial development, technology transfer and economic growth. The French ambassador invited the chief minister to visit France to explore opportunities for expanding bilateral trade and economic relations.

 CM Maryam Nawaz thanked him for the invitation and expressed her interest in strengthening commercial and industrial ties between the two sides.

The meeting also focused on Pakistan’s GSP+ status and its significance for the country’s exports and industrial economy. The chief minister described the preferential trade arrangement as a lifeline for Pakistan’s exports, particularly for Punjab’s textile, garments, sports goods and leather industries, which depend heavily on access to European markets.

She stressed that France’s support was important for safeguarding Pakistan’s trade interests within the European Union and maintaining preferential access for Pakistani products. She said alignment with the requirements of the new GSP+ framework was essential for securing the country’s export prospects.

Govt expands free hepatitis C screening and treatment programme to GB, AJK

Maryam Nawaz noted that the European Union was Pakistan’s largest trading partner, with Pakistan’s exports to the bloc reaching approximately $8.96 billion in 2025-26. She underscored the importance of continued diplomatic engagement with France to strengthen Pakistan’s position on GSP+ and further consolidate trade relations with the EU.

Recalling France’s previous support for Pakistan’s GSP+ status at the ministerial level, CM Punjab expressed confidence that continued French cooperation would help protect Pakistan’s commercial interests in European markets.

The Material Enabling New Possibilities Across Industries

The chief minister also thanked France for providing a €180 million loan for National Transmission and Despatch Company (NTDC) transmission lines and grid stations in Punjab, acknowledging the contribution towards strengthening the province’s energy infrastructure.

She invited French investors to benefit from investment opportunities in the Urban wastewater governance project planned for major cities of Punjab, highlighting the potential for international partnerships in urban infrastructure and environmental management.

Identifying specific areas of cooperation, Maryam Nawaz said French dairy, food-processing and cold-chain companies could help modernize agriculture and add value in Punjab. French utility companies could participate in water supply, wastewater management, sewerage and solid waste services under the public-private partnership model.

She further said French energy companies could explore opportunities in solar energy, grid infrastructure and energy-efficiency projects in industrial estates, while French institutions could assist in technical training and skills development for Punjab’s workforce through industrial clusters under PIVOT.

The CM observed that PIVOT could provide an effective platform for establishing direct institutional links between Punjab and France, creating new opportunities for industrial collaboration, investment and development partnerships.

Emphasising the longstanding friendship between Pakistan and France, Maryam Nawaz said the two countries shared decades of diplomatic relations and common aspirations for cooperation. Referring to the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, she appreciated France’s historic contribution to the principles of liberty, equality and human dignity.

She also commended France’s recognition of Palestine and its principled position on justice and equal rights.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations through sustained diplomatic engagement, increased trade, investment and industrial partnerships and cooperation in mutually beneficial areas of economic development.

headline: Riots erupt in Paris as more than 300,000 march across France

author: NEWS WIRE
article_text:
PARIS - The French government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday in demonstrations focused on high living costs, fewer than in previous demonstrations.

Mass protests Oct. 17 drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are much higher. The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

Thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. Some 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches on both Oct. 17 and Oct. 24.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, a few thousand people started gathering Saturday afternoon behind a line of students who were set to lead the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France’s largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed in side streets. The marchers’ grievances are diverse. Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from “Thriller,” a pirate and a Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said he lives in a state-run student residence where “there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.” He said he hoped Saturday’s protest would be festive in honor of Halloween, to counter the image of violence that has attached itself to France’s protests.

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday’s marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred entry to Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in many cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but as of Saturday afternoon only several thousands marched in various cities across the country.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

Thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. Some 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches on both Oct. 17 and Oct. 24.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, a few thousand people started gathering Saturday afternoon behind a line of students who were set to lead the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France’s largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed in side streets. The marchers’ grievances are diverse. Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from “Thriller,” a pirate and a Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said he lives in a state-run student residence where “there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.” He said he hoped Saturday’s protest would be festive in honor of Halloween, to counter the image of violence that has attached itself to France’s protests.

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday’s marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred entry to Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in many cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but as of Saturday afternoon only several thousands marched in various cities across the country.

headline: Past in Perspective
description: George Eastman changed human history and revolutionised photography with his invention of the Kodak camera in 1888. Unlike its predecessors, the Kodak was
author: The Nation
article_text: George Eastman changed human history and revolutionised photography with his invention of the Kodak camera in 1888. Unlike its predecessors, the Kodak was portable, easy to use, and affordable, employing roll film instead of cumbersome glass plates. This democratised photography, making it accessible to the masses and marking the birth of snapshot photography. Eastman’s innovation paved the way for modern photography, influencing visual culture, journalism, and personal expression. Today, the ubiquity of smartphone cameras echoes Eastman’s vision of making photography accessible to all. His invention continues to shape how we capture and share moments, highlighting the enduring impact of his greatest work.

headline: A Failure of Safety
description: The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) is one of Islamabad’s largest public hospitals, treating patients from across the country. An
author: The Nation
article_text:
The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) is one of Islamabad’s largest public hospitals, treating patients from across the country. An institution of this importance must not only treat illness but also guarantee safety and dignity.

On 26 August 2026, a devastating fire reportedly broke out in the children’s hospital at PIMS, claiming the lives of 15 newborn babies. An inquiry committee reportedly attributed the tragedy to systemic institutional failures, with an electrical fault identified as the likely cause. Newborns are among the most vulnerable patients, entirely dependent on hospital staff and safety systems. The inquiry reportedly found that 15 medically fragile babies were being cared for in a 10-bed nursery, with no functional smoke detectors, fire alarms or sprinkler system. There was also no properly rehearsed fire evacuation plan.

This raises serious questions about safety standards in public hospitals. Fire-safety equipment, emergency exits and evacuation procedures must be regularly inspected, and staff must receive practical training. Concerns raised before the tragedy, including reports of an earlier fire at the PIMS nursing hostel in July 2026, also warrant attention. The lives lost cannot be restored, but such a tragedy must not be forgotten. The government should conduct a comprehensive safety audit of hospitals, ensure transparent accountability and make patient safety a priority rather than an afterthought.

Healthcare is not just about treatment; it is also about protecting human life. The PIMS tragedy must prompt stronger safety standards across Pakistan’s healthcare system.

SPOZMI KIBZAI,

Loralai.

headline: Climate Change and Agriculture
description: Many families in Turbat and the surrounding areas depend on agriculture for their livelihoods. However, rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, drought and
author: The Nation
article_text:
Many families in Turbat and the surrounding areas depend on agriculture for their livelihoods. However, rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, drought and water shortages are making farming increasingly difficult.

Extreme heat can damage crops and increase their water requirements, placing further pressure on farmers who already struggle to secure sufficient irrigation. Unpredictable rainfall creates additional problems: prolonged dry spells can weaken crops, while heavy downpours may damage farmland and wash away fertile soil.

Water scarcity is another major concern. Farmers who depend on wells, water pumps and other irrigation sources face rising costs when water levels fall. Reduced agricultural production can place considerable financial pressure on farming families.

Livestock is also vulnerable to extreme heat and shortages of water and animal feed. Furthermore, declining crop yields can reduce the availability of agricultural produce and push up food prices, affecting the wider community.

Practical support is urgently needed. Relevant departments should provide farmers with guidance on climate-resilient crops, efficient irrigation, water conservation and improved farming methods. Repairing water systems, protecting existing water sources and promoting water-efficient techniques could help communities manage limited resources.

Local communities can also contribute by planting trees, protecting existing vegetation and conserving water. However, lasting progress requires cooperation between government departments, agricultural experts and farmers.

Agriculture supports livelihoods and the local economy. With better planning, improved water management and practical government assistance, Turbat’s farming communities can become better prepared for changing climatic conditions.

FATIMA NAEEM,

Turbat.

headline: Mobile Phones Effect on Children
description: Excessive mobile phone use can harm children’s physical and mental well-being. Screen addiction is an increasing concern, as prolonged use can distract
author: The Nation
article_text:
Excessive mobile phone use can harm children’s physical and mental well-being. Screen addiction is an increasing concern, as prolonged use can distract children from their studies and reduce their interaction with family members.

Many children return from school and spend four or five hours scrolling on their phones instead of completing assignments, eating properly or participating in outdoor activities. As a result, physical play and family interaction are neglected, while concentration and academic performance may suffer. Some students even arrive at school feeling tired and sleepy.

Parents sometimes give children mobile phones to keep them quiet or occupied without considering the long-term consequences of excessive screen time.

Parents must set reasonable limits on phone use and encourage children to read, play outdoors and spend quality time with their families. Schools can also promote awareness of healthy digital habits.

Mobile phones can be useful educational tools, but their excessive use should not come at the expense of children’s health, learning and development.

ZABID SALAM,

Lahore.

Excessive mobile phone use can harm children’s physical and mental well-being. Screen addiction is an increasing concern, as prolonged use can distract children from their studies and reduce their interaction with family members.

Many children return from school and spend four or five hours scrolling on their phones instead of completing assignments, eating properly or participating in outdoor activities. As a result, physical play and family interaction are neglected, while concentration and academic performance may suffer. Some students even arrive at school feeling tired and sleepy.

Parents sometimes give children mobile phones to keep them quiet or occupied without considering the long-term consequences of excessive screen time.

Parents must set reasonable limits on phone use and encourage children to read, play outdoors and spend quality time with their families. Schools can also promote awareness of healthy digital habits.

Mobile phones can be useful educational tools, but their excessive use should not come at the expense of children’s health, learning and development.

ZABID SALAM,

Lahore.

headline: Pakistan’s TTP Quagmire
description: The killing of Counter-Terrorism Department Deputy Superintendent of Police Imranuddin Khan and three colleagues—Sub-Inspector Afzal Awan, Constable
author: Fawad Hussain Chaudhry
article_text:
The killing of Counter-Terrorism Department Deputy Superintendent of Police Imranuddin Khan and three colleagues—Sub-Inspector Afzal Awan, Constable Kazim, and Bomb Disposal Unit Head Constable Amjad—in a gun battle in Karak district on 22 October 2026 is the latest grim marker in a conflict that has claimed thousands of lives over more than two decades. The officers died during a search-and-strike operation against suspected militants linked to a commander named Qaiser Iqbal. Imranuddin, a frontline CTD officer who had survived earlier attacks and refused safer postings, embodied the continuity of this war: the same network that targeted senior police leadership years earlier continues to hunt those who confront it.

This is not a new war. It is the latest chapter in a series of conflicts that have defined Pakistan’s tribal frontier since the colonial campaigns of the 1920s and earlier. The current phase has clear roots in the decisions taken after 11 September 2001. When al-Qaeda struck New York, President George W. Bush framed the choice for Pakistan in stark terms: “You are either with us or against us.” Islamabad aligned with the United States, reversing its long-standing support for Afghan mujahideen groups that had fought the Soviet Union. Not everyone in the tribal areas accepted the reversal. The frontier divided into what were sometimes called “good” Taliban—those who stayed with the Pakistani state—and “bad” Taliban who joined the Afghan resistance, particularly the Haqqani network.

The Haqqanis take their name from Darul Uloom Haqqania in Akora Khattak, the major Deobandi seminary in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa whose alumni include key Afghan Taliban and Haqqani figures. The network maintained deep tribal and educational ties on the Pakistani side of the border while fighting first the Soviets and then the Americans. After the US withdrawal in 2021 left both sides of the border angry, impoverished, and devastated, the Afghan Taliban’s return to power created new openings.

In government at the time, we received a briefing at ISI headquarters from then Director General Lt Gen Faiz Hamid. He conveyed a message from the Haqqanis: to settle the terrorism problem in the tribal areas, they proposed a truce with Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The Haqqanis would mediate if TTP fighters and their families were allowed to return and settle in their own villages in Pakistan. Both Prime Minister Imran Khan and Army Chief Gen Qamar Javed Bajwa saw an opportunity to end a draining conflict by bringing home people who had left to wage jihad against the United States.

Imran Khan took the proposal to a meeting at the Prime Minister’s House with the Chief Minister, ministers and PTI affiliates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He expected broad support for what seemed a practical way to wind down the war. Instead, the room was unanimous in opposition. Noor-ul-Haq Qadri, the federal Minister for Religious Affairs and a prominent tribal leader from the Khyber area, was blunt: the people being discussed had killed members of his family, and the blood debt would be settled. Others, including Murad Saeed, also rejected the idea. Two structural obstacles made reconciliation almost impossible. First, years of fighting had left both sides with dead relatives—brothers, fathers and others—making forgiveness politically and socially explosive. Second, local residents had already occupied the houses and lands abandoned by those who crossed into Afghanistan; they had no intention of surrendering them.

When the government suggested resettling the returnees in other areas rather than their home villages, the Haqqanis refused outright. In Pashto terms, this amounted to bakhur—a form of dishonour. The fighters and their tribes would view them as pakhar, outsiders stripped of standing if they could not return to their own soil. Negotiations were still underway when the government was removed in 2022.

The conflict is now fully active again. The Afghan Taliban, particularly elements close to the Haqqani network, provide the TTP with sanctuary, facilitation, and operational space inside Afghanistan. Pakistani security forces and police continue to absorb losses in operations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the former tribal districts, while the TTP and affiliated groups sustain attacks. The brief window for a negotiated return and local resettlement closed without resolution, and the underlying tribal, familial, and territorial grievances remain.

The future offers no easy exit. Pure military pressure has not eliminated the threat so long as cross-border sanctuary persists. Pure negotiation collides with the same blood feuds, property disputes and honour calculations that blocked the earlier proposal. Any durable path will require sustained pressure on the Afghan Taliban to end TTP facilitation, tighter border management, selective local reconciliation only where communities actually accept it, and serious economic and administrative investment in the districts that have borne the heaviest cost. Without addressing both the external sanctuary and the internal fractures, the cycle that has run from the 1920s through the post-9/11 years and into the present will continue to produce new names—Imranuddin Khan among the latest—on the list of those killed by the same enemy.

Now the conflict has acquired a very strong sectarian element as well. In earlier phases—against the Soviet Union and later the United States—the war was framed essentially as a struggle between Muslims and non-Muslims. That framing no longer holds. Today it is a far more complex internal conflict among Muslim factions. Salafi groups, drawing from former al-Qaeda networks and Daesh/ISKP, are actively targeting Deobandi ulema and institutions, particularly those associated with Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (JUI-F), as well as TTP and Afghan Taliban factions. Attacks on Deobandi seminaries, political rallies and scholars have become a recurring pattern, driven by deep ideological hostility between Salafi and Deobandi schools of thought.

This is no longer simply a war between Muslims and non-Muslims. It is a multi-layered sectarian struggle involving Shia, Deobandi and Salafi factions, overlaid on the enduring tribal warfare of the borderlands. The addition of this sectarian dimension has further complicated any path to resolution, multiplying the actors, the grievances and the incentives for continued violence.

To control the ongoing violence, coercive measures remain important because hardline fighters understand little else. Yet coercion alone is not the answer. What is required is a multi-layered approach with strategies that vary from one local area to another. In some districts, the sectarian conflict is more lethal than the tribal one; in others, tribal rivalries and blood feuds dominate. Effective decisions demand a clear understanding of local populations, local interests and local problems. A uniform national template will fail where the drivers of violence differ sharply from valley to valley and tribe to tribe.

The non-cooperation of the Afghan Taliban remains a huge hurdle. These violent groups in Pakistan’s tribal areas now enjoy vast territory inside Afghanistan where they can hide, plan, store weaponry, and train suicide bombers—the primary instrument of destruction used by these factions. The war therefore needs both international cooperation and sustained domestic cooperation. Political support, especially local political support, is sine qua non. The imposition of governor’s rule further complicates the issue: whatever limited political support the state retained in these areas is now eroded. Pakistan needs political stability and domestic backing at the Union Council level to fight this war. Without it, the conflict will linger, producing thousands of additional casualties on top of the thousands already suffered.

Fawad Hussain Chaudhry The writer is the former Information Minister of Pakistan.

In government at the time, we received a briefing at ISI headquarters from then Director General Lt Gen Faiz Hamid. He conveyed a message from the Haqqanis: to settle the terrorism problem in the tribal areas, they proposed a truce with Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The Haqqanis would mediate if TTP fighters and their families were allowed to return and settle in their own villages in Pakistan. Both Prime Minister Imran Khan and Army Chief Gen Qamar Javed Bajwa saw an opportunity to end a draining conflict by bringing home people who had left to wage jihad against the United States.

Imran Khan took the proposal to a meeting at the Prime Minister’s House with the Chief Minister, ministers and PTI affiliates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He expected broad support for what seemed a practical way to wind down the war. Instead, the room was unanimous in opposition. Noor-ul-Haq Qadri, the federal Minister for Religious Affairs and a prominent tribal leader from the Khyber area, was blunt: the people being discussed had killed members of his family, and the blood debt would be settled. Others, including Murad Saeed, also rejected the idea. Two structural obstacles made reconciliation almost impossible. First, years of fighting had left both sides with dead relatives—brothers, fathers and others—making forgiveness politically and socially explosive. Second, local residents had already occupied the houses and lands abandoned by those who crossed into Afghanistan; they had no intention

of surrendering them.

When the government suggested resettling the returnees in other areas rather than their home villages, the Haqqanis refused outright. In Pashto terms, this amounted to bakhur—a form of dishonour. The fighters and their tribes would view them as pakhar, outsiders stripped of standing if they could not return to their own soil. Negotiations were still underway when the government was removed in 2022.

The conflict is now fully active again. The Afghan Taliban, particularly elements close to the Haqqani network, provide the TTP with sanctuary, facilitation, and operational space inside Afghanistan. Pakistani security forces and police continue to absorb losses in operations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the former tribal districts, while the TTP and affiliated groups sustain attacks. The brief window for a negotiated return and local resettlement closed without resolution, and the underlying tribal, familial, and territorial

grievances remain.

The future offers no easy exit. Pure military pressure has not eliminated the threat so long as cross-border sanctuary persists. Pure negotiation collides with the same blood feuds, property disputes and honour calculations that blocked the earlier proposal. Any durable path will require sustained pressure on the Afghan Taliban to end TTP facilitation, tighter border management, selective local reconciliation only where communities actually accept it, and serious economic and administrative investment in the districts that have borne the heaviest cost. Without addressing both the external sanctuary and the internal fractures, the cycle that has run from the 1920s through the post-9/11 years and into the present will continue to produce new names—Imranuddin Khan among the latest—on the list of those killed by the same enemy.

Now the conflict has acquired a very strong sectarian element as well. In earlier phases—against the Soviet Union and later the United States—the war was framed essentially as a struggle between Muslims and non-Muslims. That framing no longer holds. Today it is a far more complex internal conflict among Muslim factions. Salafi groups, drawing from former al-Qaeda networks and Daesh/ISKP, are actively targeting Deobandi ulema and institutions, particularly those associated with Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (JUI-F), as well as TTP and Afghan Taliban factions. Attacks on Deobandi seminaries, political rallies and scholars have become a recurring pattern, driven by deep ideological hostility between Salafi and Deobandi schools of thought.

This is no longer simply a war between Muslims and non-Muslims. It is a multi-layered sectarian struggle involving Shia, Deobandi and Salafi factions, overlaid on the enduring tribal warfare of the borderlands. The addition of this sectarian dimension has further complicated any path to resolution, multiplying the actors, the grievances and the incentives for continued violence.

To control the ongoing violence, coercive measures remain important because hardline fighters understand little else. Yet coercion alone is not the answer. What is required is a multi-layered approach with strategies that vary from one local area to another. In some districts, the sectarian conflict is more lethal than the tribal one; in others, tribal rivalries and blood feuds dominate. Effective decisions demand a clear understanding of local populations, local interests and local problems. A uniform national template will fail where the drivers of violence differ sharply from valley to valley and tribe to tribe.

The non-cooperation of the Afghan Taliban remains a huge hurdle. These violent groups in Pakistan’s tribal areas now enjoy vast territory inside Afghanistan where they can hide, plan, store weaponry, and train suicide bombers—the primary instrument of destruction used by these factions. The war therefore needs both international cooperation and sustained domestic cooperation. Political support, especially local political support, is sine qua non. The imposition of governor’s rule further complicates the issue: whatever limited political support the state retained in these areas is now eroded. Pakistan needs political stability and domestic backing at the Union Council level to fight this war. Without it, the conflict will linger, producing thousands of additional casualties on top of the

thousands already suffered.

Fawad Hussain Chaudhry

The writer is the former Information Minister of Pakistan.

headline: Most Important Election
description: The Michigan Senate race between the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, and his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, is this year’s most important
author: Dr. James J. Zogby
article_text:
The Michigan Senate race between the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, and his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, is this year’s most important election.

It’s significant on a number of levels, including that El-Sayed is an Arab American Muslim of Egyptian descent. Prior to this, we’ve had four Arab Americans elected to the US Senate, none of them Muslim.

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first—a breakthrough not lost on Republicans and President Trump, who are determined to exploit it at every turn. They’ve done TV adverts alleging that El-Sayed’s mother was affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1970s. The problem with this charge is that El-Sayed’s parents separated when he was three; she moved back to Egypt and he grew up with his father in Michigan. But facts don’t matter when tarnishing a candidate is the goal. The GOP has persisted in spreading the Muslim Brotherhood lie on social media and through paid hecklers at El-Sayed’s campaign events. A recent exchange of this sort backfired on the Republican instigators.

At a town hall, a young man asked whether El-Sayed would denounce the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed shot back, “Yes, absolutely,” then pivoted, asking the questioner, “Why are you asking me this?”—was it because of his name or how he prayed? El-Sayed made clear that the document to which he’d take an oath was the US Constitution and smartly compared the attacks against him with those levelled against President Kennedy—that Kennedy would be more loyal to the Catholic Pope than to the Constitution. El-Sayed concluded, noting that he wasn’t running to be a Muslim senator, but a senator who happened to be a Muslim.

That exchange went viral on social media, drawing more than 50 million viewers the first night. The next day, it was revealed that the heckler was a former staffer for a very conservative anti-Muslim Senator, who’d been hired to disrupt El-Sayed events. This illustrates another reason why this election is so important: the role of dark money in American politics. Dark money refers to money raised by “super PACs” and independent expenditure funds that aren’t required to report donors before elections. It allows billionaires and special interest groups to amass and spend large sums defaming candidates who oppose their agendas. Increasingly, these dark money sources are raising and spending more on campaigns than the candidates themselves.

In the primary, El-Sayed was confronted by dark money expenditures of $70 million ($31 million from pro-Israel groups). Despite being outspent 11 to 1, El-Sayed won. In the general election, an estimated $100 million in dark money will be spent against him. His victory would demonstrate dark money’s limits and advance the argument that it should be banned for its corrosive role in our democracy.

From the campaign’s beginning, El-Sayed has clearly and consistently criticised US support for the Israeli genocide in Gaza—explaining why so much pro-Israel super PAC money was spent to defeat him. His Democratic primary opponent made support for Israel central to her campaign. Pro-Israel Jewish organisations denounced El-Sayed and did their best to tarnish him, labelling him antisemitic. While this succeeded in costing El-Sayed some support from Jewish American Democratic voters, he won the primary.

In the general, El-Sayed is being confronted by the same attacks and organised efforts by the same pro-Israel groups. El-Sayed has stated that instead of spending billions to buy bombs to kill Palestinians, America’s wealth should be building better schools and providing health care. Once a taboo topic, it’s resonated with Democrats and independent voters.

Finally, an El-Sayed victory will succeed in advancing a progressive agenda. Despite being attacked as a socialist, he maintains that he wants capitalism to work for the people. His arguments are simple: It shouldn’t be easier for a billionaire to make another billion than for a family to be lifted out of poverty. Health care is a human right, not a privilege only affordable for some. Instead of spending billions on wars, we must invest in schools and the quality of life here at home.

These are the challenges El-Sayed presents to our politics. If he wins, he’ll have succeeded in shattering taboos and raising issues that will have a lasting impact. Even if he loses, our politics will never be the same. On so many levels, it’s a historic, transformative campaign.

Dr. James J. Zogby The writer is the President of Arab American Institute.

headline: Beyond Emergency Relief
description: Tharparkar suffers from repeated droughts. The desert needs a long-term plan focused on water security, resilient livelihoods, healthcare and education, rather
author: Ali Nawaz Rahimoo
article_text:
Tharparkar suffers from repeated droughts. The desert needs a long-term plan focused on water security, resilient livelihoods, healthcare and education, rather than emergency assistance each time the monsoon fails.

In south-eastern Sindh, rain is the basis of life. It determines whether crops grow, livestock survive and families can sustain themselves. When the monsoon fails, the consequences extend beyond farming to drinking water, food security, children’s education, and physical and mental health. Each drought brings the same challenges: water shortages, loss of grazing land and livestock, and migration. Why does a region repeatedly facing drought still lack a comprehensive plan to protect its people before the next crisis?

Tharparkar has experienced severe dry periods in the 1960s, 1980s, late 1990s and early 2000s, followed by a prolonged crisis from 2013 to 2018. Covering 19,638 square kilometres and home to approximately 1.78 million people, according to the 2023 census, its scattered settlements and limited water resources make public service delivery difficult. Its dependence on rainfall leaves communities particularly vulnerable.

Agriculture and livestock remain central to local livelihoods. Farmers depend on monsoon rains to grow millet, guar and sesame, while grazing lands sustain goats, sheep, cattle and other animals. Insufficient rainfall damages crops, depletes grazing fields and increases fodder costs. Livestock represent more than income; they are a family’s financial security during difficult times. Distress sales and depleted savings undermine recovery and deepen vulnerability.

Migration to irrigated areas of Sindh in search of fodder, grazing land and temporary employment has long been a coping mechanism. However, displacement comes at a social cost. Children miss school, families lose access to essential services, and women, older people and persons with disabilities face additional barriers to healthcare and clean water.

Water scarcity remains a fundamental development challenge. Communities rely on rainwater, groundwater, wells and local tanks, many of which become unreliable during prolonged dry periods. In some areas, groundwater is either too deep or unsuitable for drinking.

Drought also disrupts education and healthcare. Financial hardship and migration force children to miss lessons or leave school altogether. School retention programmes, targeted household assistance and continuity arrangements for mobile families must be strengthened, alongside nutrition and social protection services.

Remote villages often lack adequate healthcare facilities and staff. Poor roads, muddy tracks and limited emergency transport delay referrals, particularly for pregnant women, children and seriously ill patients. Investment in rural health facilities, staff recruitment and retention, four-wheel-drive ambulances, all-weather roads and mobile health teams is essential.

The psychological toll of drought also demands attention. Debt, crop failure, livestock losses and uncertainty heighten distress. Media reports recorded 122 deaths by suicide in Tharparkar between January and September 2026. While suicide cannot be attributed to drought alone, vulnerable communities need accessible counselling, trained frontline health workers, referral services and public awareness initiatives to reduce stigma. Mental healthcare must become part of primary healthcare rather than an emergency afterthought.

The government of Sindh needs to replace reactive relief with a coordinated programme that reduces the impact of drought before household resources are exhausted. A district-level early-warning system should integrate rainfall forecasts, vegetation conditions, groundwater data, crop assessments and livestock health reports. Clear thresholds must trigger timely assistance, including food support, fodder, veterinary care and emergency water supplies.

Livestock protection should remain central to drought preparedness. Community fodder banks, vaccination campaigns, mobile veterinary teams and accessible animal health services can prevent losses. Assistance must be sufficient to prevent distress sales and protect breeding animals.

Livelihood diversification is equally important. Support for enterprises, women-led businesses, drought-resilient agriculture, livestock value chains, vocational training and local employment can reduce dependence on a single rainy season. Tharparkar’s mineral resources and cultural heritage offer opportunities, but development must generate meaningful employment and benefits for surrounding communities.

Social protection must also integrate education, nutrition and healthcare, ensuring children remain in school, pregnant women access essential services and temporary economic shocks do not become long-term deprivation.

The proposed Thar Development Authority merits consideration as a mechanism for coordinating long-term investment. The government should review the proposal, consult local com munities and technical experts, and determine whether a dedicated authority would improve coordination, accountability and implementation.

If established, it must have a clear legal mandate, defined responsibilities, transparent budgeting and measurable targets. Its work should integrate water management, livestock development, climate-resilient agriculture, healthcare, education, infrastructure and livelihood diversification. Local government representatives, community organisations, women and relevant technical departments must participate meaningfully in planning and monitoring. Annual public reports should disclose expenditure, beneficiaries and project outcomes. The authority must complement existing institutions rather than duplicate their responsibilities, with success measured by improvements in people’s lives, not the establishment of offices or announcement of schemes.

The people of Tharparkar have generations of experience adapting to their environment. Their knowledge, livelihoods and cultural traditions must inform development planning. However, communities cannot be expected to withstand recurring uncertainty without reliable public services and sustained investment.

Drought will remain a recurring risk in this arid region, but its consequences need not be as devastating. The real test of government policy is whether a failed monsoon still forces families to sell livestock, abandon homes or face shortages of food, water and healthcare.

Tharparkar needs more than wheat subsidies and fodder distribution after every drought. It needs a sustained commitment to water security, resilient livelihoods, accessible public services and accountable institutions. The time has come to move from recurring emergency relief towards long-term development that protects livelihoods and preserves the dignity of the people of Thar.

Ali Nawaz Rahimoo The writer is a social development professional and can be reached at anrahimoo@gmail.com
